Both describe a claimant or property owner seeking special legislative treatment despite an existing general administrative regime, emphasize the large number of similarly situated parties, characterize preferential treatment as discriminatory or unjustified, and warn that granting the exception would invite further special legislation that would undermine orderly general procedures. C13 has a similar preference-and-precedent argument, while C14 parallels the preference for completing a comprehensive program over granting narrow benefits, but neither matches the child as closely as C04.","shared_material":[{"child_excerpt":"We should not single out two of these now by special legislation and provide benefits for them which cannot be enjoyed by any of the other many nonconforming uses.","parent_excerpt":"There are thousands of other debt claims equal or higher in priority to Colonel Cunningham's. It would clearly be discriminatory to place this claim in a preferred position.","explanation":"Both reject legislation that selects a small number of beneficiaries from a much larger similarly situated class and gives them preferential treatment."},{"child_excerpt":"To do so would constitute an invitation for other special legislative exceptions","parent_excerpt":"To set aside the procedures prescribed by general law would lead other claimants to seek special legislation to speed the settlement of their claims.","explanation":"This is a distinctive shared precedent-warning: one special exception would encourage additional parties to seek comparable special legislation."},{"child_excerpt":"The Board of Commissioners of the District of Columbia and the National Capital Planning Commission have had underway for the past three years a study looking to a complete revision of the Zoning Regulations... That study is almost completed","parent_excerpt":"The provisions of that Act were designed to provide orderly and equitable procedures for the distribution of vested enemy property. I do not believe these procedures should be ignored","explanation":"Each memorandum contrasts the proposed individualized relief with an existing or nearly completed general process intended to resolve the wider class of cases in an orderly manner."}]}
